title: Decimal Expansions
subtitle: Which fractions stop, and which repeat forever

meta.seo_title: Terminating vs Recurring Decimals — Predict It Without Dividing

blocks.narration: Welcome back to Math Concepts Made Easy. This is Day 3, and by the end of it you will know whether a fraction terminates without dividing at all.
Let's quickly recap Day 2. We proved that the square root of two is not a fraction, we met irrational numbers, and we learned that a decimal is only rational if it stops or repeats.
blocks.heading: Day 2 — what we proved
items: √2 cannot be written as p over q

blocks.narration: Compare these two. One half is nought point five and it stops dead. One third is nought point three three three and it never stops at all. Same kind of fraction, completely different behaviour.

The whole answer is hiding in the denominator. Reduce the fraction first, then factorise the bottom. If the only prime factors are twos and fives, the decimal terminates. Any other prime, and it recurs forever.
blocks.headline: Look only at the denominator

blocks.narration: Here is why. Our number system is built on powers of ten, and ten is two times five. If the denominator is made only of twos and fives, you can always scale it up into a power of ten, and a power of ten is what a terminating decimal is.
blocks.title: Why twos and fives

blocks.narration: Try it. Sort these by their denominators alone: seven over forty, five over twelve, nine over twenty five, and one over six.
Last one. Does thirteen over sixty four terminate? Pause and check the denominator before I say a word.
blocks.question: Does 13/64 terminate?

blocks.narration: So you never have to divide again to know how a fraction behaves. Tomorrow, in Day 4, we turn a recurring decimal back into a fraction using one clever trick with algebra. See you then.
